S13v9-1P2: Don't combine ownership/major resources until the group has had at least one real conflict and dealt with it all the way through. Not "dealt with it" by writing a vision statement and shaking hands, or declaring a truce nobody believes, but really dealing with it. In other words, you need to do some real relational pl/ork where someone names what happened and each person gets time. What comes up in the conflict is jealousy, humiliation, fear, or old material, and you find out which. Deal with it until the emotional pressure has changed enough for an agreement to mean something, and then you can make one. Otherwise, what's it worth?
S13v9-2P1: Have you noticed people often choose their community in the same way they would choose a vacation rental? “Wow! Look at this beautiful land! And a pond, with the sunset in it!! Who needs a beach?! And the people seem really nice, let’s get in here!” Fast forward two years. “Wait, there’s a vaccination policy?? And you need paperwork for it?!?!”

S13v9-3P4: Good people leave for good reasons, like a dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, or just a simple change of mind. Leaving should not require someone to leave everything they’ve put in, as that’s effectively coercing someone to stay. You should write down the exit terms while no one is leaving yet, and it’s still just a theoretical discussion. Think of it as a pre-nup while you’re planning the wedding. It’s not that romantic, but it’s protective, and a lot easier than doing it when people are furious.

For the order to do all this in, see Diana Leafe Christian’s Creating a Life Together: First you get the vision, then you get the members, then you pool the major resources, and lastly you get the land. So yes, the land comes last!
S13v9-4P4: The long visit: If you're not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you're not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months, so time gets you more evidence, not certainty.
S13v9-4P6: How do you know? At each stage, always judge people based on their conduct. No matter how good it sounds when they talk about their spirituality or their therapy, don’t go by that. It’s too easy to go by vibes. It’s also easy to mistake people just doing what everyone else is doing for safety. Even giving it six months will give you more data, but it won’t tell you if someone is a good person.
